title: Object-ball throw versus cut angle and shot speed
purpose: Validates the 1/7 sticking constant, the Coulomb cap on the tangential impulse and the speed-dependent friction coefficient. Every row is at one of TP A.14's own speeds, so that the model and the measurement beside it are the same shot. Also records the size of the residual against the measurement (see known_deviations).
sources: Alciatore, 'The Amazing World of Billiards Physics' (2007), TP A-14 throw data

params.note: object ball placed along the cut-angle bisector per row; the cue ball is spinless, so the slip is purely horizontal and the slip speed is the cue ball's speed times sin(cut)

known_deviations: The residual is at most half a degree over the whole sweep (the worst row is a 30 degree cut at 7 mph, at 0.48 degrees). It is not one-sided: in the slow columns the model sits slightly ABOVE the measurement (up to +0.2 degrees at a 30 degree cut) and in the faster columns up to 0.5 degrees BELOW it. The shortfall below the measurement grows with the speed, except at a 60 degree cut where the medium speed is the peak. In the sticking regime (10 degrees) it agrees with the measurement to 0.03 degrees.

An earlier version of this fixture recorded a degree-wide offset and claimed the three columns at a 30 degree cut could not be fitted by any law of the form A + B exp(-K u). That claim turned the measured throw into an implied friction coefficient with mu = tan(throw), which is valid only in the sliding regime: the slow column (4.65 degrees) sits at the 4.83 degree sticking limit, where the throw does not depend on the friction coefficient at all, so it gives only a LOWER bound on it. Taking the sticking branch into account, TP A.14's own law reproduces all three columns to within half a degree (doc section 14.3).
The measured throw depends on the cue ball's spin as well as its speed, and the published figures do not carry every shot condition (doc section 14.3).
